fixes.explanation: That's right, baker. Nehemiah says, "For they were all trying to frighten us…" (Nehemiah 6:9) What they said was that the Jews' hands would be weakened in the work and it would never be finished. So all those messages had one aim: to scare.

It's true, friend. Nehemiah says, "For they were all trying to frighten us…" (Nehemiah 6:9) What they said was that the Jews' hands would be weakened in the work and it would never be finished. All those messages had a purpose.

Susa is where Nehemiah's story starts (Nehemiah 1:1), so I see why it came to mind. But Sanballat and Geshem name a village on the plain of Ono (Nehemiah 6:2). Sanballat and Geshem are two enemies of Nehemiah, the man rebuilding Jerusalem's wall. Nobody is inviting him to a palace here, and I think a fancy address would have made the invite look even better.

I'd have loved for that to be true, friend, but the text says otherwise. Right after the invite, it says, "But they were planning to harm me." (Nehemiah 6:2) Sanballat and Geshem, two of Nehemiah's enemies, sent an invite with a plan to harm him behind it. A meeting on the plain of Ono was never as friendly as it sounded.

Yes, baker. Nehemiah answers, "I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it to go down to you?" (Nehemiah 6:3) He's talking to Sanballat and Geshem, two enemies who want him to come down. He doesn't argue or explain his whole life. He gives one reason, the work, and asks one question.

I get it, you'd think four invites would wear him down. But the text says, "…each time I gave the same reply." (Nehemiah 6:4) Nehemiah's reply doesn't change, even as the invites keep coming from his enemies. Same reply, every time.

Not longer, friend. Nehemiah says it outright: "…each time I gave the same reply." (Nehemiah 6:4) The text calls it the same reply each time, and it never says he stretched it out. I think after the first answer he already had it ready to go.

Look again, baker. The text says the servant had "…an unsealed letter" in his hand (Nehemiah 6:5). Unsealed is the word the text uses, so the letter was not sealed. The writer doesn't say why, so I won't guess.
Right, baker. Sanballat's young servant had "…an unsealed letter" in his hand (Nehemiah 6:5). So the letter was not sealed. The text doesn't tell us why, so I'll leave that alone.

Not quite, friend. The letter doesn't say priest. It says, "…you are to become their king…" (Nehemiah 6:6) The letter claims that you and the Jews are plotting to revolt, and Nehemiah says Sanballat made it all up (Nehemiah 6:8).

Yes, baker. Nehemiah writes back, "There is nothing to these rumors you are spreading; you are inventing them in your own mind." (Nehemiah 6:8) He doesn't go looking for who started it. He tells Sanballat, the enemy who sent the letter, that he made it up himself. Short and to the point, and no meeting required.

That's right, baker. Shemaiah, a man confined to his house, says, "Let us meet at the house of God inside the temple. Let us shut the temple doors…" (Nehemiah 6:10) His warning is that they're coming to kill Nehemiah by night. Notice he's asking Nehemiah to go inside and shut the doors.

That's right, baker. Nehemiah says he realized God had not sent Shemaiah, but "…that he had uttered this prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him." (Nehemiah 6:12) So the warning sounded holy but was paid for. Sanballat is the same enemy who sent the earlier letter (Nehemiah 6:5).

That would make Shemaiah an honest mistake, but the text gives a different reason. Nehemiah says Shemaiah gave the prophecy "…because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him." (Nehemiah 6:12) The reason the verse gives is the hiring, not a rumor. Nehemiah also realized God had not sent him.
Yes, baker. The text says, "So the wall was completed in fifty-two days…" (Nehemiah 6:15) That's a little over seven weeks. The verse even gives the date: the twenty-fifth of Elul.
Ninety is a bigger number than the text gives. It says, "…the wall was completed in fifty-two days…" (Nehemiah 6:15) Fifty-two days, not ninety.
Forty is a close guess, but this verse says, "…the wall was completed in fifty-two days…" (Nehemiah 6:15) Fifty-two, not forty. Twelve more days, and every one of them counted.

That's right, baker. The text says, "…all the surrounding nations were afraid and disheartened…" (Nehemiah 6:16) That was their reaction once all the enemies heard the wall was done. The text says, "…they realized that this task had been accomplished by our God."
Joyful isn't the word the text uses. It says, "…all the surrounding nations were afraid and disheartened…" (Nehemiah 6:16) That was their reaction once all the enemies heard the wall was done.

It's true, friend. The text says, "For many in Judah were bound by oath to him…" (Nehemiah 6:18) Tobiah, one of Nehemiah's enemies, had ties with many in Judah. The verse explains it with two family ties: he was a son-in-law of Shecaniah son of Arah, and his son Jehohanan had married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah.

That's right, baker. The text says, "…these nobles kept reporting to me Tobiah’s good deeds, and they relayed my words to him." (Nehemiah 6:19) Tobiah is the enemy from earlier in the chapter. The nobles of Judah told Nehemiah about his good deeds and passed Nehemiah's words on to him.
